questions.question: For open subsets $(\boldsymbol{E}_i)_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ of a metric space, what does the proposition say about $\bigcup_{i = 1}^{\infty}\boldsymbol{E}_i$?
options: It is closed but not open.
It is open only if the sets are finite.

questions.question: For open subsets $\boldsymbol{E}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{E}_k$, what does the proposition say about $\bigcap_{i = 1}^{k}\boldsymbol{E}_i$?
options: It is necessarily closed but not open.

questions.question: Which operation on open sets is guaranteed to preserve openness only in the finite case in the proposition?
Which stronger statement is true for open sets?
options: Any intersection of open sets is open, even for uncountable families.
Any union of open sets is open, even for uncountable families.
Only finite unions of open sets are open.
Open sets are preserved only under pairwise unions.

questions.question: A student claims that $\bigcap_{n = 1}^{\infty}(-\frac{1}{n},1+\frac{1}{n})$ is open because every set in the intersection is open. What is the error?
options: The theorem only guarantees finite intersections of open sets.
Openness is never preserved by intersections, not even for two sets.

questions.question: Which two sets are always open in a metric space?
Let $U$ and $V$ be non-empty open proper subsets of $\mathbb{R}$. Which claim is false?
Which set is an infinite intersection of open sets that is not open in $\mathbb{R}$?

For open sets $E_1,\dots,E_k$ and a point $x$ of $E_1\cap\dots\cap E_k$, balls of radii $\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_k$ around $x$ lie inside the respective $E_i$, and a ball of radius $\min_i\varepsilon_i>0$ lies inside the intersection. Why does this argument fail for an infinite intersection $\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty}E_i$?
options: The radii $\varepsilon_i$ may have infimum $0$, so no single ball around $x$ fits inside all the $E_i$.
A point $x$ of the intersection need no longer be an interior point of each individual $E_i$.
With infinitely many sets $\inf_i\varepsilon_i$ is still positive, but it is no longer attained by any one $E_i$.
The argument does not fail: the intersection of any family of open sets is open by the same reasoning.

questions.question: Let $G_1,G_2,G_3,\dots$ be open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$. What can be said about $\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}G_n$?
options: It need not be open, but it can be: $\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}(-n,n)=(-1,1)$ is open, while $\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}(-\tfrac{1}{n},\tfrac{1}{n})=\{0\}$ is not.
It is never open: with infinitely many sets the balls that fit inside always shrink to nothing, as for $\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}(-\tfrac{1}{n},\tfrac{1}{n})=\{0\}$.
It is always open: the proposition on intersections of open sets applies to any family, as $\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}(-n,n)=(-1,1)$ illustrates.
It is open if and only if the sets are nested, $G_1\supseteq G_2\supseteq G_3\supseteq\cdots$.
